To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the chemical form of Se is spatially resolved at a resolution of 100 microm; (2) the chemical form and concentration of selenium in the roots and shoots of A. bisulcatus can be quantified with a spatial resolution of 100-300 microm; and (3) the chemical form, concentration, and spatial distribution of selenium in A. bisulculus are developmentally regulated.

(i) we have demonstrated the ability to quantitatively image specific chemical forms of a biologically important element in intact tissues of plants, (ii) we have shown that the ability to transform selenate to organoselenium is developmentally specific in the plant tissue, and (iii) we have shown the ability to quantitate and spatially resolve the chemical form of Se at 100 microm resolution.

(1) the ability of Astragalus bisculatus to accumulate selenate is developmentally and spatially regulated in the root and shoot; (2) Astragalus bisclatus is capable of accumulating selenate to concentrations in excess of 0.5 mM in mature leaves, a concentration far greater than that found in the roots; and (3) the ability to accumulate selenite in roots is highly localized to specific regions of the root tip.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel x-ray technique to study chemical speciation in plants and other biological systems.
the development of a new imaging technique that is applicable to biological systems and the application of this technique to the study of the bioinorganic transformations of Se in the plant kingdom.

the development of a novel imaging method that can be used to study the distribution of trace elements in biological systems and with the application of this method to study the bioinorganic transformation of Se in plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chemical form of Se is dependent upon both tissue age and location.
the chemical forms of Se in plants are not homogeneous but rather highly spatially resolved and heterogeneous.
selenate is the predominant chemical species in the mature leaves and the roots of A. bisulcatus plants, and that the roots contain a small but significant amount of organoselenium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemical form and concentration of Se can be quantified at the micrometer level, and that the chemical form is developmentally regulated.

we have demonstrated the ability to image the chemical form of an element in a biological system, and that the spatial distribution of Se in A. bisulcatus is consistent with the hypothesis that the plant uses selenate as a source of organoselenium.
the ability of A. bisulcatus to biotransfer selenate into organoselenium is both inducible and developmentally specific, and that this ability is localized in the root extremities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
x-ray fluorescence imaging at the Se K-edge can be used to quantitatively map the chemical distribution of Se at the cellular and subcellular levels in biological samples.
the combination of synchrotron radiation and advanced data analysis techniques can provide quantitative, chemically specific, and high-spatial-resolution images of biological tissues.
the combination of synchrotron radiation and a scanning x-ray microscope provides a powerful new tool for studying chemical transformations in intact plant tissues at the micron scale.
